subject: Copywriting
subcategory: The Science of Storytelling in Ads
title: The Hero's Journey in Ads
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Hero's Journey in Ads usable.

hook.text: Luke Skywalker's journey: ordinary world, call to adventure, mentor, trials, victory. Nike uses this exact template.

buildup.text: Joseph Campbell identified the monomyth in 1949. George Lucas used it for Star Wars. Brands adopted it for advertising.

discovery.text: In Nike ads, the customer is the hero. The shoe is the magical weapon. Nike itself is the mentor guiding you.

twist.text: Most brands make the mistake of casting themselves as the hero. The customer must be the hero—the brand is the guide.

climax.text: Apple, Nike, Airbnb—all position the customer as hero. The brand doesn't save the day; it equips you to save it.

punchline.text: The customer is the hero. The brand is just the guide.

quiz.question: In ad storytelling, who should be the hero?

details.summary: Joseph Campbell's Hero's Journey — departure, initiation, return — provides the narrative structure behind some of the most successful ads ever made. The customer is the hero, the brand is the guide, and the product enables the transformation. This framework makes ads feel epic and meaningful.
details.whyItMatters: The Hero's Journey gives advertisers a proven narrative framework that resonates across cultures. When customers see themselves as the hero of the story, the brand's role as enabler creates emotional loyalty that transcends rational comparison.
takeaways: The customer should always be the hero, not the brand
The brand serves as the mentor or guide that enables the hero's transformation
The Hero's Journey structure creates emotional arcs that feel universally satisfying

faq.question: How does the Hero's Journey apply to a 30-second ad?
faq.answer: Compress the arc: show the hero (customer) facing a challenge, encountering the guide (brand), using the tool (product), and achieving transformation. Nike's ads do this brilliantly — ordinary person faces obstacle, puts on Nike shoes, conquers the challenge.

faq.question: Why should the brand be the guide, not the hero?
faq.answer: Donald Miller's StoryBrand framework clarifies this: customers don't care about the brand's story — they care about their own. Brands that position themselves as the hero create self-congratulatory ads. Brands that position themselves as the guide create ads that empower the customer.
